new.title: See the Mean Ruz lighthouse among pink granite
new.desc: The Ploumanac'h lighthouse, officially Mean Ruz, is a small light built of pink granite that marks the channel into the harbour of Ploumanac'h. The present tower dates from after the war, replacing the one destroyed in 1944. The tower itself is closed to visitors, but the setting among the boulders is the best-known image of the Pink Granite Coast.
new.tip: Come at sunset or at low tide, and walk the customs path from the Saint-Guirec oratory. The Maison du Littoral nearby has documentation on the site.
new.q: Phare de Ploumanac'h (Mean Ruz), Ploumanac'h, Perros-Guirec

new.title: Walk to the Paon lighthouse on Bréhat
new.desc: The Phare du Paon stands on a rocky promontory at the northern tip of the Île de Bréhat. It was rebuilt in 1949 in red porphyry after the original was destroyed in the Second World War, and it lines up with the Rosédo light. Walking there from the village takes about an hour each way.
new.tip: Cross from Pointe de l'Arcouest and go on foot or by bike, as cars are not allowed. Combine it with the Croix de Maudez on the west coast.
new.q: Phare du Paon, Île de Bréhat

new.title: Explore the maritime Abbey of Beauport
new.desc: Beauport Abbey is a former Premonstratensian abbey founded in 1202 with the help of Alain I d'Avaugour, count of Penthièvre and Goëlo. Its ruins and gardens sit on the edge of Paimpol bay at Kérity, and it is now a departmental heritage site. It was suppressed in 1790.
new.tip: Check opening hours before going. Tibus bus line 9 links the abbey with Paimpol and Saint-Brieuc stations.
new.q: Abbaye de Beauport, Kérity, Paimpol

new.title: Admire the three towers of Tréguier cathedral
new.desc: Saint-Tugdual cathedral in Tréguier was the seat of one of Brittany's nine historic dioceses until 1790. The Gothic building, mostly 13th to 15th century, is known for three towers over the transept, each in a different style, and for its Gothic cloister.
new.tip: Visit the cloister as well, and pair it with the Renan house a few streets away. Address: Place du Martray.
new.q: Cathédrale Saint-Tugdual, Place du Martray, Tréguier

new.title: Visit the childhood home of Ernest Renan
new.desc: Built at the end of the 16th century, this typical Trégor house was bought in 1780 by the grandparents of the historian Ernest Renan, who left Tréguier at 15. It became a museum in 1947 and is run by the Centre des monuments nationaux as a Maison des Illustres.
new.tip: Open seasonally (April to September in 2026), so check before going. Admission is free for visitors under 26 from the EU.
new.q: Maison d'Ernest Renan, 20 rue Ernest Renan, Tréguier

new.title: See the rood screen at Kerfons chapel
new.desc: The chapel of Kerfons-en-Kerfaouës near Lannion was destroyed in the War of the Succession and rebuilt in the 15th and 16th centuries. It is protected as a historic monument and holds a late 15th-century rood screen and a Renaissance wing dated 1559.
new.tip: Entry has been around 2 euros, free for under-12s. Verify the opening season locally.
new.q: Chapelle de Kerfons, Chemin de Kerfons, Ploubezre

new.title: Climb through the ruins of Tonquédec castle
new.desc: Tonquédec is a ruined medieval castle on a ridge above the Léguer valley, with eleven towers and a closed curtain wall. It was dismantled on Richelieu's orders in 1626 and is listed as a historic monument. It is privately owned and one of the most visited sites in the Côtes-d'Armor.
new.tip: The owners open it from April to October. A 7 km walking loop starts nearby.
new.q: Château de Tonquédec, Tonquédec

new.title: Stroll the French gardens of Rosanbo
new.desc: The Château de Rosanbo has been open to visitors since 1958. Its park was laid out by Achille Duchêne and features a salle de verdure, a parterre, topiary, a labyrinth, sphinx statues and a water mirror. It carries the Jardin remarquable label.
new.tip: The park can be visited alone or with the château. Check seasons on rosanbo.net.
new.q: Château de Rosanbo, Lanvellec

new.title: Step inside the Radôme at the Cité des Télécoms
new.desc: The Radôme in Pleumeur-Bodou housed the antenna that received the first live US television pictures in July 1962 via Telstar. It was classed a historic monument in 2000, and the Cité des Télécoms museum around it covers two centuries of telecommunications in nine themed spaces.
new.tip: The park also holds the Planétarium de Bretagne. Evening projections on the dome are held in summer.
new.q: Cité des Télécoms, Parc du Radôme, Pleumeur-Bodou

new.title: Visit the Notre-Dame de la Clarté chapel
new.desc: This 15th-century chapel in Perros-Guirec was listed as a historic monument in 1915, and its spire once served sailors as a landmark. It is the centre of the annual Pardon de la Clarté.
new.tip: The pardon takes place in summer. The chapel is a short walk from the town centre.
new.q: Chapelle Notre-Dame de la Clarté, Place de la Chapelle, Perros-Guirec

new.title: Look over the bay from the Tour de Cesson
new.desc: The Tour de Cesson is the surviving keep of a fortress built between 1395 and 1407 for Duke Jean IV of Brittany. The castle covered about 3 hectares and was dismantled twice. It stands on a 70 m hill above the Gouët mouth and the bay of Saint-Brieuc, and was registered in 1926.
new.tip: Walk up for the view over the Anse d'Yffiniac. The city recently acquired the tower, so check access.
new.q: Tour de Cesson, 1 chemin de l'Écluse, Saint-Brieuc

new.title: Enter the fortress-cathedral of Saint-Brieuc
new.desc: Saint-Étienne cathedral is one of the rare fortress-cathedrals in Brittany, rebuilt several times after attacks. It has been a historic monument since 1906, and the Saint-Guillaume chapel holds the tomb of bishop Guillaume Pinchon. A long restoration finished in February 2026.
new.tip: Admission is free; guided visits run mainly in summer.
new.q: Cathédrale Saint-Étienne, Saint-Brieuc

new.title: Wander the ramparts and lanes of Moncontour
new.desc: Moncontour is a hilltop medieval town and a Petite Cité de Caractère. Its main monument is the church of Saint-Mathurin with a Renaissance bell tower and listed 16th-century stained glass.
new.tip: Follow the heritage trail through the lanes and see the stained glass in the church.
new.q: Église Saint-Mathurin, Moncontour

new.title: See the Black Madonna in Guingamp basilica
new.desc: The Basilica of Notre-Dame-de-Bon-Secours began as a castle chapel of the counts of Penthièvre and became a parish church in the 12th century. It holds a Black Madonna, a labyrinth and an organ case of 1654, and has been a basilica since 1899.
new.tip: Entry is free. The pardon of Notre-Dame-de-Bon-Secours is held each year.
new.q: Basilique Notre-Dame de Bon-Secours, Guingamp

new.title: Scramble over the granite chaos of the Corong gorges
new.desc: The Gorges du Corong is a chaos of granite boulders where the Follezou stream disappears under the rocks and reappears as a waterfall. Local legend says a giant named Boudédé scattered the stones. It sits by the Landes de Locarn.
new.tip: Park at the Corong car park and walk down to the rocks. Wear shoes with grip.
new.q: Gorges du Corong, Locarn

new.title: Visit the Cistercian ruins of Bon-Repos abbey
new.desc: Bon-Repos is a Cistercian abbey founded in 1184 beside the Nantes-Brest canal, close to the Guerlédan lake. Its ruins have been restored and host exhibitions and, in summer, a sound-and-light show.
new.tip: Combine it with a walk on the canal towpath or around the lake.
new.q: Abbaye de Bon-Repos, Bon Repos sur Blavet

new.title: Tour the towers of Fougères castle
new.desc: Fougères is a medieval fortress of about two hectares with a dozen towers, often presented as Europe's largest. Sources date the first castle to around the year 1000, with the stone fortress rebuilt after 1166. The Mélusine and Gobelins towers are among the oldest.
new.tip: The fortress runs medieval animations and a family audioguide. Check seasonal hours.
new.q: Château de Fougères, Place Pierre Symon, Fougères

new.title: Explore the Château de Vitré and its museum
new.desc: The castle, where the town hall also sits, has a museum in the Saint-Laurent, Argenterie and Oratoire towers. It was listed in 1872 and the museum opened in 1877. It dominates the half-timbered old town.
new.tip: Closed on Tuesdays and on weekend mornings from October to March. Prices are about 7 to 10 euros.
new.q: Château de Vitré, Place du Château, Vitré

new.title: Tour Chateaubriand's castle at Combourg
new.desc: The château de Combourg, beside Lac Tranquille, is where François-René de Chateaubriand spent his youth and lodged in the Tour du Chat. It is privately owned, listed as a historic monument and open as a memorial to the writer.
new.tip: Check seasons on chateau-combourg.com. The park around the lake is also pleasant.
new.q: Château de Combourg, Combourg

new.title: Browse the book town of Bécherel
new.desc: Bécherel is a medieval village about 30 km from Rennes and France's first Cité du Livre, a title it has held since 1989. It has around fifteen bookshops, binders and book artisans.
new.tip: Most shops are open Thursday to Sunday. A secondhand book market is held on the first Sunday of most months.
new.q: Bécherel, Cité du Livre, Bécherel

new.title: Walk through La Roche-aux-Fées dolmen
new.desc: This Neolithic passage tomb at Essé, dated roughly 3000 to 2500 BC, is built of schist slabs with a trilithic porch. It was classified as a historic monument in 1840, and legend says fairies built it.
new.tip: The monument is about 30 km south-east of Rennes. Trails for walking and cycling start nearby.
new.q: La Roche-aux-Fées, Essé

new.title: Visit Saint-Sauveur abbey church in Redon
new.desc: The abbatiale Saint-Sauveur next to the town hall mixes Romanesque and Gothic architecture, with medieval frescoes and cloisters. Tradition says the abbey was founded in 832 by the monk Conuvoion with support of Louis the Pious.
new.tip: Combine with the port, where the canal from Nantes to Brest meets the Vilaine.
new.q: Abbatiale Saint-Sauveur, Place Saint-Sauveur, Redon

new.title: Tour the donjon of Châteaugiron castle
new.desc: The castle at Châteaugiron has a 38 m keep that houses the Gourdel museum, devoted to the sculptors Julien and Pierre Gourdel. It is visited with a guide only, and the donjon needs a specific tour.
new.tip: Book the L'indémodable or La nocturne tour to climb the donjon. Contact the tourist office for dates.
new.q: Château de Châteaugiron, Châteaugiron

new.title: Wander the Parc botanique de Haute-Bretagne
new.desc: This 25-hectare garden at Le Châtellier, created in 1847 around the Foltière château, has 24 thematic gardens and more than 7,000 species, including a Persian-style garden. It has the Jardin remarquable label.
new.tip: Open roughly March to mid-November. Adult admission is about 9 to 11 euros.
new.q: Parc botanique de Haute-Bretagne, La Foltière, Le Châtellier

new.title: Visit Madame de Sévigné's Rochers estate
new.desc: The Château des Rochers-Sévigné near Vitré was the Breton home of Madame de Sévigné, who stayed several times after her husband's death. The French garden dates from 1689 on a design attributed to Le Nôtre and was restored in 1982. The Sévigné family owned it for about three centuries from 1410.
new.tip: Open as a château-museum; check seasonal hours. Address: route d'Argentré-du-Plessis.
new.q: Château des Rochers-Sévigné, route d'Argentré-du-Plessis, Vitré

new.title: Eat galettes at Crêperie des Flots in Perros-Guirec
new.desc: Crêperie des Flots on the Perros-Guirec harbour was founded in 2014 by chef Sébastien Élie. It is rated highly by diners and often recommended for galettes and crêpes with local products.
new.tip: Book ahead, as reviews advise. Try a galette with local seafood or a salted-butter caramel crêpe.
new.q: Crêperie des Flots, Port, Perros-Guirec

new.title: Try galettes at Ty Breizh in Perros-Guirec
new.desc: Ty Breizh, in rue de Landerval, is listed by Gault&Millau for galettes and crêpes made with carefully sourced products. Reviews rate it at about 4.5 out of 5.
new.tip: Go outside peak hours and ask for the daily galette. Check seasonal opening.
new.q: Ty Breizh, rue de Landerval, Perros-Guirec

new.title: Dine on crêpes at Le Bistrot du Port, Ploumanac'h
new.desc: Le Bistrot du Port in Ploumanac'h serves homemade galettes and crêpes from fresh produce, a short walk from the pink granite shoreline and lighthouse.
new.tip: Pair it with the coastal walk to the Mean Ruz lighthouse.
new.q: Le Bistrot du Port, Port de Ploumanac'h, Perros-Guirec

new.title: Order scallops at Le Terre Neuvas on Paimpol harbour
new.desc: Le Terre Neuvas stands on the port of Paimpol, a town tied to the Newfoundland cod fishery. Diners praise the welcome, the terrace and the scallops and oysters.
new.tip: Ask for the scallops of the bay and sit on the terrace. Expect to pay around 60 euros for a full meal.
new.q: Le Terre Neuvas, quai Morand, Paimpol

new.title: Taste Coco de Paimpol at La Table du Marché, Tréguier
new.desc: La Table du Marché in Tréguier is Michelin-listed and serves roast cod with Coco de Paimpol, the protected white bean grown around Paimpol.
new.tip: Book ahead for dinner. Visit the Saturday market the same morning.
new.q: La Table du Marché, Place du Martray, Tréguier

new.title: Eat galettes at Crêperie Le Moulin Vert in Lannion
new.desc: Le Moulin Vert on rue Duguesclin in Lannion specialises in buckwheat galettes and crêpes, close to the old half-timbered streets of the town.
new.tip: Combine it with a walk past the timber-framed houses of rue des Chapeliers.
new.q: Crêperie Le Moulin Vert, rue Duguesclin, Lannion

new.title: Eat Erquy scallops at La Table de Jeanne
new.desc: La Table de Jeanne, open since 2014, is an emblematic restaurant on Erquy harbour. Its menu includes seared scallops from the bay, which Erquy lands as one of Europe's main scallop ports.
new.tip: Go from October to May for fresh scallops in season. Book for evenings.
new.q: La Table de Jeanne, Port d'Erquy, Erquy

new.title: Taste scallops tataki at La Paillote, Erquy
new.desc: La Paillote is a bar-restaurant-rumhouse on the harbour whose seafood comes from the nearby Erquy fish auction. Scallops are served in several ways, including poached, marinated, pan-seared and as tataki.
new.tip: Sit on the harbour side and ask for the scallop of the day.
new.q: La Paillote, Port d'Erquy, Erquy

new.title: Try the seaweed galette at Crêperie des Promenades
new.desc: This small family crêperie in central Saint-Brieuc is known for its complete galette, its galette with seaweed and sweet crêpes.
new.tip: Reserve, as the room is small.
new.q: Crêperie des Promenades, 18 rue des Promenades, Saint-Brieuc

new.title: Book a table at Crêperie Bleu Marine, Saint-Brieuc
new.desc: Crêperie Bleu Marine on rue Aristide Briand is a Saint-Brieuc institution, a few minutes' walk from the centre and the railway station.
new.tip: Booking is strongly advised.
new.q: Crêperie Bleu Marine, 28 rue Aristide Briand, Saint-Brieuc

new.title: Eat buckwheat galettes at La Broustal, Fougères
new.desc: La Broustal is a mother-and-son crêperie at 102 rue de la Pinterie in the old town, open seven days a week, with a terrace facing the old town and vegetarian and gluten-free options.
new.tip: Ask for the terrace seats across the street.
new.q: La Broustal, 102 rue de la Pinterie, Fougères

new.title: Watch crêpes being made at Crêperie Tivabro, Fougères
new.desc: Tivabro is a well-reviewed crêperie on Place du Marchix in a 16th-century building in the medieval quarter, where you can watch the crêpes being cooked. It is listed by Gault&Millau.
new.tip: Booking is advisable.
new.q: Crêperie Tivabro, Place du Marchix, Fougères

new.title: Buy buckwheat galettes at La Maison du Sarrasin, Fougères
new.desc: La Maison du Sarrasin at 73 rue de la Pinterie is a crêperie known for its galettes of buckwheat flour, and it also operates as a grocery.
new.tip: Take home buckwheat flour and spreads.
new.q: La Maison du Sarrasin, 73 rue de la Pinterie, Fougères

new.title: Taste chocolates at Bruno Le Derf in Vitré
new.desc: Bruno Le Derf is a chocolatier-pâtissier at 21 rue Duguesclin in Vitré, led by a Meilleur Ouvrier de France. Next door at number 25 there is a tea room where the pastries can be eaten.
new.tip: Look for the local Vitréais cake, made with caramelised apple and almonds.
new.q: Chocolatier Pâtissier Bruno Le Derf, 25 rue Duguesclin, Vitré

new.title: Try a chestnut galette at Crêperie l'Akène, Redon
new.desc: L'Akène at 10 rue du Jeu de Paume in Redon is a traditional crêperie that has offered chestnut dishes during the town's October chestnut month, such as a galette with sausage, chestnut and onion jam.
new.tip: Come in October for the chestnut specials.
new.q: Crêperie l'Akène, 10 rue du Jeu de Paume, Redon

new.title: Drink coffee at Gwrizienn café-librairie, Bécherel
new.desc: Gwrizienn is a café and bookshop in the book town of Bécherel.
new.tip: Pair it with a browse through the antiquarian bookshops, most open Thursday to Sunday.
new.q: Gwrizienn Café Librairie, 3 rue de la Chanvrerie, Bécherel

new.title: Eat crêpes by the lake at La Fée Gourmande, Paimpont
new.desc: La Fée Gourmande, at 16 avenue du Chevalier Ponthus on the shore of the Paimpont lake, opened in 2010 and is praised for its lakeside terrace and view.
new.tip: Take a table on the terrace after a forest walk.
new.q: Crêperie La Fée Gourmande, 16 avenue du Chevalier Ponthus, Paimpont

new.title: Hike the customs path from Saint-Guirec to Ploumanac'h
new.desc: The GR34 customs path through the pink granite chaos is one of the best-known hikes in Brittany. The usual route runs from Trestraou beach in Perros-Guirec past Saint-Guirec to the Mean Ruz lighthouse, roughly 9 km round trip.
new.tip: Start early for light and avoid high tide. The Maison du Littoral sells a booklet on the geology for 2 euros.
new.q: Plage de Saint-Guirec, Ploumanac'h, Perros-Guirec

new.title: Sail to the Sept-Îles bird reserve from Perros-Guirec
new.desc: Armor Navigation runs trips from Perros-Guirec's Trestraou maritime station to the Sept-Îles archipelago, with a 40-minute stop on Île aux Moines. Rouzic island has the richest seabird colony in metropolitan France, with gannets and, until mid-July, puffins, and grey seals.
new.tip: Trips run April to September. Check the current timetable with the operator.
new.q: Gare maritime de Trestraou, Perros-Guirec

new.title: Take the Vedettes de Bréhat ferry from l'Arcouest
new.desc: Vedettes de Bréhat run the roughly 10-minute crossing from Pointe de l'Arcouest at Ploubazlanec, about 5 km beyond Paimpol, to the car-free island. Tickets are open with no fixed time and the service runs all year.
new.tip: Bikes go over until 9:30 and return until 16:00. Check the timetable on vedettesdebrehat.com.
new.q: Pointe de l'Arcouest, Ploubazlanec

new.title: Ride the Vapeur du Trieux steam train
new.desc: This tourist steam train runs between Paimpol and Pontrieux along the Trieux estuary, about twenty kilometres in an hour, with a locomotive classed as a historic monument. The 2026 season ran from 14 June to 15 September.
new.tip: Confirm the departures with the operator. Family tickets are around 58 to 60 euros.
new.q: Gare de Paimpol, Paimpol

new.title: Walk the Sillon de Talbert shingle spit
new.desc: The Sillon de Talbert is a long shingle spit at Pleubian that points towards Bréhat. A round trip of about 5.9 km from the Maison du Sillon takes about an hour and a half and is easy. Entry is free.
new.tip: Check tide times, as a channel cuts across the route.
new.q: Maison du Sillon de Talbert, Pleubian

new.title: Cross to Île Milliau at low tide from Trébeurden
new.desc: Île Milliau can be reached on foot from Trébeurden across a ford of about a hundred metres, only at low tide. It has a 5,000-year-old gallery grave and a walk of about an hour around the island.
new.tip: The town hall and tourist office publish crossing times; check them. Leave margin for the return, as the tide comes in fast.
new.q: Port de Trébeurden, Trébeurden

new.title: Shop the Thursday market in Lannion
new.desc: Lannion's main market takes place on Thursdays, with stalls spreading through the old streets from the quai d'Aiguillon to Place du Marchallac'h, near the half-timbered houses.
new.tip: Go in the morning. Check hours with the town hall.
new.q: Place du Général Leclerc, Lannion

new.title: Cycle the Vilaine towpath from Redon to Messac
new.desc: The Redon to Messac stretch of the Saint-Malo to Arzal cycle route follows the Vilaine river and canal. Redon sits at the junction of the Vilaine, the Oust and the Nantes-Brest canal.
new.tip: Start at the port of Redon. Boat rentals for the canal are also available in Redon.
new.q: Port de Redon, Redon

new.title: Walk around the heather of Cap d'Erquy
new.desc: The Cap d'Erquy site covers about 170 hectares of heath and pink sandstone cliffs and has been protected since 1978. A 7.6 km loop called Les plages sauvages circles the cape in about two hours, starting from Caroual beach.
new.tip: Best in April and May for heather colour. Parking at the point is limited.
new.q: Plage de Caroual, Erquy

new.title: Stroll the Val-André sea wall
new.desc: The digue-promenade at Val-André runs in front of the Saint-Symphorien beach, about 2 to 2.5 km long between the Murs-Blancs and Piégu points. The sea wall was built in the second quarter of the 20th century.
new.tip: The digue is pedestrian only. Walk it at sunset.
new.q: Digue promenade du Val-André, Pléneuf-Val-André

new.title: Swim at Plage du Châtelet in Saint-Quay-Portrieux
new.desc: The Châtelet beach lies between the casino beach and the Sémaphore point, sheltered by a cliff, near the town centre, with beach huts and a free seawater pool on the left of the beach.
new.tip: The beach is not supervised. Cafés line the esplanade above.
new.q: Plage du Châtelet, Saint-Quay-Portrieux

new.title: Join a guided bird walk at the Maison de la Baie
new.desc: The Maison de la Baie at Hillion is the nature centre of the Saint-Brieuc bay reserve, classified in 1998 and covering 1,140 hectares of mudflats, dunes and salt marsh. It offers guided walks, and access to most of the reserve along the GR34 is free.
new.tip: Book guided walks by phone or email.
new.q: Maison de la Baie, Site de l'Étoile, Hillion

new.title: Walk the ponds of Paimpont abbey and Pas du Houx
new.desc: A 7 km easy loop from Paimpont links the Abbey pond and the 65 to 70 hectare Pas du Houx pond, the largest water body in the Brocéliande forest. Paimpont abbey is a listed Benedictine monastery dating from the 13th century.
new.tip: Start at the abbey car park. Paths cross heath and boardwalks.
new.q: Abbaye de Paimpont, Paimpont

new.title: Hike the Porte de Brocéliande from Montfort-sur-Meu
new.desc: The trail La porte de Brocéliande starts at the Tour du Papegault in Montfort-sur-Meu and runs along the Meu to the Saint-Jacques abbey, about 11 km in about 2h45.
new.tip: Montfort is a Petite Cité de Caractère. Visit the tower first.
new.q: Tour du Papegault, Montfort-sur-Meu

new.title: Walk or cycle around Lac de Guerlédan
new.desc: Guerlédan, created by a hydroelectric dam, is the largest artificial lake in Brittany, between the Quénécan forest and Bon-Repos. A walking loop of about 37 km circles it and La Vélodyssée cycle route passes by Mûr-de-Bretagne.
new.tip: Pick a shorter section from Mûr-de-Bretagne. Kayaks can be hired in summer.
new.q: Lac de Guerlédan, Mûr-de-Bretagne

new.title: Watch scallops land at Erquy harbour
new.desc: Erquy is called the capital of the scallop, with a fleet of about 80 trawlers fishing the bay of Saint-Brieuc. From November to March visitors can watch the unloading from the car park near the cale before the criée sale, and guided visits of the criée are advertised.
new.tip: Check the guided visit dates with the tourist office.
new.q: Port d'Erquy, Erquy

new.title: Hike the Plouha cliffs to Bréhec
new.desc: The cliffs of Plouha have the highest cliffs in Brittany, peaking at 104 m on the Pointe de Plouha along a 15 km coast. A loop starts at Bréhec beach and returns by the GR34.
new.tip: Check path conditions and the tide at Gwin Zegal.
new.q: Pointe de Plouha, Plouha

new.title: Walk around Île Renote at Trégastel
new.desc: A short coastal loop from Coz Pors circles the Île Renote peninsula past Grève Blanche, Grève Rose and the beaches of Curés and Toul Bihan. It is easy and nearly flat, and the GR34 passes here.
new.tip: Mind the tide. The car park on Île Renote is open to cars and bikes.
new.q: Parking de l'île Renote, route de l'Île Renote, Trégastel

new.title: Walk the Gouët and Gouédic valleys to Le Légué
new.desc: A marked walk starts at the Pont de pierre at Le Légué, descends through the Gouédic valley and passes under the Gouët viaduct. The Gouédic valley is a green belt through the heart of Saint-Brieuc.
new.tip: Park at Le Légué port. Part of the route runs through wooded valley.
new.q: Pont de pierre, Le Légué, Saint-Brieuc

new.title: Swim at Coz Pors beach, Trégastel
new.desc: Coz Pors is a sheltered sandy beach on the Pink Granite Coast with the GR34 customs path along it. It is supervised in July and August.
new.tip: Combine it with the aquarium and the Île Renote walk.
new.q: Plage de Coz Pors, Trégastel
